fatal_errors: The cited evidence concerns conventional tensile properties from room temperature to 1023 K and does not establish improved performance under dynamic or high-strain-rate loading.

The proposed grain-boundary-strengthening mechanism is unsupported and inconsistent with the cited evidence, which instead attributes strengthening to FCC particles pinning superdislocations inside L12 precipitates.
The experiment specifies neither strain rate nor a controlled processing route, so it cannot decisively attribute any dynamic strength–ductility change to the hierarchical architecture.
explanation: This is a scientifically plausible precipitation-engineering alternative, and the cited paper supports an FCC/L12/FCC hierarchical architecture with elevated yield strength and useful tensile elongation. It does not reconstruct the target intervention, which varies crystallographic loading direction, temperature, and molecular-dynamics strain rate in single-crystal equiatomic FeNiCrMn. It also misses the target mechanism of vacancy-assisted Shockley-partial nucleation, stacking-fault formation, temperature softening, and strain-rate-dependent dislocation density. The claimed dynamic benefit is an extrapolation beyond the supplied evidence. The baseline is underspecified with respect to composition, heat treatment, grain structure, and precipitate volume fraction, while the boundary is only a temperature interval. A decisive test would require composition- and processing-matched specimens, explicit dynamic strain rates, quantitative strength and failure-strain predictions, and microscopy or diffraction capable of separating precipitate pinning from grain-size and phase-fraction effects.
